- **Timing:** the game builds the line and takes the stone when queued commands next run. Stone needed by buildings, ammunition or repairs queued in the same pause is not set aside, so if those leave too little the game ends the line short.
- **Refused when:** the kind is not one of the four; the line is diagonal or too long; a tile is off the map or not free; stairs do not start beside an own wall; a crenel tile does not touch a wall; or stone is short.
- **Afterwards:** a `build_refused` event with `tiles` and `built` is recorded if fewer tiles than ordered became wall.

```python
game.build_wall(230, 210, 240, 210)
# {"queued": "wall", "tiles": 11, "stone": -5, "note": "built when game time next moves"}
game.build_wall(235, 211, 235, 214, kind="stairs")
```

See also: [`delete_wall`](#delete_wall); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#build_wall).


## `delete_wall`

Remove one owned wall tile. [API reference](../api.md#delete_wall).

- **Arguments:** `(x, y)` must be a wall or stairs tile owned by the player.
- **Effect and timing:** the tile is removed when time next moves and the game refunds half of its stone (half of that again for a low wall); a single tile's refund can round down to nothing.
- **Limits:** only walls. A moat plan is removed with `plan_moat(..., dig=False)`; pitch ditches, towers and gatehouses are buildings and are removed with `demolish`.
- **Refused when:** the tile is not one of the player's wall tiles.

```python
game.delete_wall(230, 210)
# {"queued": "delete_wall", "x": 230, "y": 210, "note": "removed when game time next moves; half its stone is refunded"}
```

See also: [`build_wall`](#build_wall); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#delete_wall).


## `plan_moat`

Mark, or unmark, a straight line of moat to be dug. [API reference](../api.md#plan_moat).

- **Arguments:** a horizontal or vertical line of at most 100 tiles; `dig=True` (default) marks the plan, `dig=False` removes a plan along the line.
- **Effect:** the game marks the plan with a two-tile brush on the tiles it accepts (land without buildings or walls), so the marked strip can be wider than the line. Planning costs nothing. A plan does not block anything until dug.
- **Returns:** `queued` (`"plan_moat"` or `"unplan_moat"`), `tiles` (the length of the line, not the number of tiles the game marked) and `note`.
- **Timing:** marked when time next moves.
- **Refused when:** the line is diagonal, longer than 100 tiles or leaves the map, or `dig` is not a Boolean.

```python
game.plan_moat(228, 230, 236, 230)
# {"queued": "plan_moat", "tiles": 9, "note": "marked when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [`dig_moat`](#dig_moat); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#plan_moat).


## `dig_moat`

Order units to dig out the player's moat plan. [API reference](../api.md#dig_moat).

- **Units:** archers, spearmen, pikemen, macemen, engineers and slaves.
- **Arguments:** `(x, y)` must be a tile of the moat plan, so advance at least one tick after `plan_moat` before ordering.
- **Effect:** the units walk to the plan and dig it out tile by tile, continuing along the plan. A dug tile is moat, which ground units cannot cross. Digging takes time (measured: four spearmen dug three tiles in about 600 ticks).
- **Refused when:** a listed unit cannot dig, or the tile is not part of the moat plan.

```python
game.dig_moat([101, 102], 230, 230)
# {"queued": "dig_moat", "units": 2, "x": 230, "y": 230}
```

See also: [`plan_moat`](#plan_moat); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#dig_moat).


## `fill_moat`

Order units to fill an enemy's dug moat tile. [API reference](../api.md#fill_moat).

- **Units:** the same diggers as `dig_moat`.
- **Arguments:** `(x, y)` must be a dug moat tile belonging to another team.
- **Effect:** the units carry earth into the moat until the tile is land again.
- **Refused when:** a listed unit cannot dig; the tile is not dug moat; or the moat is the player's own or an ally's. The player's own moat cannot be filled.

```python
game.fill_moat([101], 80, 70)
# {"queued": "fill_moat", "units": 1, "x": 80, "y": 70}
```

See also: [`dig_moat`](#dig_moat); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#fill_moat).


## `light_pitch`

Order archers to set one of the player's pitch ditches alight. [API reference](../api.md#light_pitch).

- **Units:** archers and Arabian archers.
- **Needs:** a `pitch_ditch` tile of the player's team at `(x, y)`; a lit `brazier` (placed with `build` on a wall or tower top) within 3 tiles of the **first** unit in `unit_ids`; and the pitch tile within the game's lighting range of that unit. The range is read from the game; in version 1.41 it is 49 tiles.
- **Effect:** the archers shoot a burning arrow into the ditch. The lit tile burns, sets adjoining pitch tiles alight, and burns units standing in it.
- **Refused when:** a listed unit is not an archer or Arabian archer; there is no friendly pitch ditch at the tile; no lit brazier is beside the first unit; or the pitch is out of range.

```python
game.build("brazier", 231, 224)  # on the wall the archers stand on
game.advance(10)
game.light_pitch([101, 102], 232, 230)
# {"queued": "light_pitch", "units": 2, "x": 232, "y": 230}
```

See also: [`build`](economy.md#build); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#light_pitch).


## `oil_duty`

Assign engineers to an owned oil smelter. [API reference](../api.md#oil_duty).

- **Arguments:** `engineer_ids` are engineers; `smelter_id` is an owned `oil_smelter`.
- **Effect:** one engineer works the smelter, which boils pitch from the stockpile into oil; the others wait and each receives a pot of boiling oil. The smelter needs pitch in the stockpile.
- **Limits:** pouring the oil is not available; see `pour_oil`.
- **Refused when:** a listed unit is not an engineer, or the building is not an owned oil smelter.

```python
game.oil_duty([101, 102], 42)
# {"queued": "oil_duty", "units": 2, "smelter_id": 42}
```

See also: [`pour_oil`](#pour_oil); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#oil_duty).


## `pour_oil`

Order engineers to pour boiling oil. Always refused by the game driver. [API reference](../api.md#pour_oil).

- **Status:** the driver cannot yet reproduce the game's pour action, so every call is refused rather than queue an order that would do nothing. The final refusal reads `pouring oil is not available yet`.
- **Earlier refusals:** the driver first checks that the listed units are engineers and that at least one carries an oil pot, so those messages can appear instead.

```python
game.pour_oil([101], 232, 236)  # raises CrusaderError
```

See also: [`oil_duty`](#oil_duty); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#pour_oil).

<!-- docs/commands/economy.md -->

# Economy commands

These commands manage construction, taxes, food, trade, recruitment and building upkeep. All of them are refused once the match has ended (`game over: ...`) or a configured tick budget is spent (`tick budget exhausted`). Unless stated otherwise a command is queued and the game applies it when time next moves, so call `advance` before reading its effect. Within one pause the driver reserves the gold, goods and peasants that queued trades and recruits will use, and treats queued building sites as occupied. IDs and coordinates in examples are illustrative.

## `build`

Place a building at the top-left tile of its footprint. [API reference](../api.md#build).

- **Arguments:** `building` is a placement name from the [buildings reference](../reference/buildings.md), which lists every footprint, cost and placement rule; `(x, y)` is the footprint's top-left tile. Use `find_sites` to get tiles the game accepts.
- **Checks, in order:** the map (every footprint tile on the map, free, level, and for farms farmable, for an iron mine on ore); the game's own placement check (adjacency, distance to the enemy and to the castle); the map's build menu; then the cost, read from the game's cost table, against the current stock of wood, stone, gold, iron and pitch. A drawbridge must also sit in front of the gate of an owned gatehouse.
- **Effect and timing:** the game takes the cost and places the building when time next moves. A staffed building then waits for a free peasant before it works.
- **Special names:** `flag_1` to `flag_4`, `heads` and `brazier` go on top of an owned wall or tower; `mangonel` and `ballista` go on a tower-top tile of an owned square or round tower that has no engine, and then need 2 engineers (`man`).
- **Refused when:** the name is not recognized; a tile fails the map check (the message names the tile and what blocks it); the game refuses the spot (the message carries the game's reason); the build menu does not offer the building; or the stock is short (the message gives the amounts needed and held).
- **Afterwards:** if the spot is no longer free when time moves, a `build_refused` event with a `reason` is recorded and nothing is charged.

```python
site = game.find_sites("woodcutter", limit=1, near=(235, 230))[0]
game.build("woodcutter", site["x"], site["y"])
# {"queued": "woodcutter", "x": 235, "y": 230, "note": "placed when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [`find_sites`](observe.md#find_sites); [buildings reference](../reference/buildings.md); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#build).


## `demolish`

Demolish an owned building. [API reference](../api.md#demolish).

- **Arguments:** `building_id` from `state()["buildings"]`.
- **Effect and timing:** the game removes the building when time next moves and refunds half of its cost. Its worker returns to the campfire.
- **Refused when:** the ID is not one of the player's buildings, or it is the keep (`the keep cannot be demolished`).
- **Afterwards:** a `demolish_refused` event is recorded if the building is still standing after time moved.

```python
game.demolish(12)
# {"queued": "demolish", "building_id": 12, "type": "woodcutter", "note": "removed when game time next moves; part of its cost is refunded"}
```

See also: [`events`](observe.md#events); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#demolish).


## `set_tax`

Set the tax level, from -3 to 8. [API reference](../api.md#set_tax).

- **Levels:** −3 to −1 are bribes paid to the population out of the treasury, 0 is no tax, 1 to 8 are increasingly heavy taxes.
- **Popularity:** each level has a fixed monthly popularity effect: −3: +7, −2: +5, −1: +3, 0: +1, 1: −2, 2: −4, 3: −6, 4: −8, 5: −12, 6: −16, 7: −20, 8: −24.
- **Gold:** tax grows with the level and the population. The game accumulates it weekly and pays it into the treasury at the end of each game month, so receipts trail a change by up to a month. Bribes are deducted the same way.
- **Timing:** the level changes when time next moves and shows as `State.tax`.
- **Refused when:** `level` is not an integer from −3 to 8.

```python
game.set_tax(1)
# {"tax": 1}
```

See also: [`report`](observe.md#report); [popularity](../concepts.md#popularity); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#set_tax).


## `set_rations`

Set the ration level: none, half, normal, extra or double. [API reference](../api.md#set_rations).

- **Popularity:** `none` −8, `half` −4, `normal` 0, `extra` +4, `double` +8 a month. With no food in the granary the effect is −8 whatever the setting.
- **Food:** higher rations empty the granary faster in proportion.
- **Timing:** the level changes when time next moves and shows as `State.rations`.
- **Refused when:** `level` is not one of the five names.

```python
game.set_rations("extra")
# {"rations": "extra"}
```

See also: [`report`](observe.md#report); [food and rations](../concepts.md#food-and-rations); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#set_rations).


## `trade`

Buy or sell goods at the market in multiples of five. Positive quantities buy; negative quantities sell. [API reference](../api.md#trade).

- **Needs:** an owned `market`, and a good the map allows to be traded. Gold itself cannot be traded.
- **Arguments:** `qty` is a non-zero multiple of 5 with an absolute value of at most 500.
- **Buying:** costs the game's current buy price per lot of 5. The driver refuses a purchase the treasury cannot cover after other spending queued in this pause. If the good's store has no room when time moves, the game buys nothing and keeps the gold.
- **Selling:** earns the current sell price per 5. The game sells in lots sized by the stock at each sale: everything below 5 in stock, 5 at a time below 50, 10 below 100, 20 below 200, otherwise 50. The requested amount must be reachable exactly with those lots; for example 15 can be sold from a stock of 40 (three lots of 5) but not from a stock of 120 (lots of 20).
- **Returns:** `queued` (`"buy"` or `"sell"`), `good`, `qty`, `gold` (negative for the cost of a purchase, positive for the proceeds of a sale) and `note`.
- **Timing:** executed when time next moves.
- **Refused when:** the good is not recognized or `cannot be traded`; `qty` is zero, not a multiple of 5 or over 500; there is no market; gold is short; or the sale cannot be made in the game's lot sizes.

```python
game.trade("wood", 10)  # buy 10 wood
game.trade("apples", -20)  # sell 20 apples
# {"queued": "sell", "good": "apples", "qty": -20, "gold": 16, "note": "sold when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [goods reference](../reference/goods.md#trading); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#trade).


## `recruit`

Recruit soldiers, mercenaries or specialists from idle peasants. [API reference](../api.md#recruit).

- **Arguments:** `unit` is a name from the [units reference](../reference/units.md), which lists every price and the goods each unit uses; `count` is 1 to 50 (default 1).
- **Needs, per recruit:** one idle peasant at the campfire (`State.idle_peasants`), the gold price, and the recruiting building: a `barracks` for archers, crossbowmen, spearmen, pikemen, macemen, swordsmen and knights; a `mercenary_post` for the seven Arabian units; an `engineers_guild` for engineers and laddermen; a `tunnelers_guild` for tunnelers; a `cathedral` for monks. Barracks troops also use one of each of their weapons and armor from the armory, and a knight uses one horse from the stables.
- **Effect and timing:** the game takes the gold and goods when time next moves. A barracks soldier appears about 40 ticks later, when his peasant has walked to the barracks; other recruits walk from the campfire to their building in the same way. The new unit then appears in `State.units`.
- **Returns:** `queued` (the unit name), `count`, `gold` (the total cost, negative) and `note`.
- **Refused when:** the unit name is not recognized; `count` is out of range; the map does not offer the unit; the building is missing; or gold, a weapon, armor, horses or idle peasants are short. The message names what is missing and how much is available after earlier commands of the same pause.

```python
game.recruit("archer", count=2)
# {"queued": "archer", "count": 2, "gold": -24, "note": "paid when game time next moves; each soldier appears at the barracks ~40 ticks later"}
```

See also: [units reference](../reference/units.md); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#recruit).


## `repair`

Repair a damaged owned tower or gatehouse to full health. [API reference](../api.md#repair).

- **Applies to:** `lookout_tower`, `perimeter_tower`, `defense_turret`, `square_tower`, `round_tower`, `gatehouse` and `large_gatehouse`. Other buildings have no repair.
- **Cost:** the game computes it from the damage: the missing share of the building's health times its wood and stone cost, at least 1 of each material the building costs. The amounts are returned as `wood` and `stone`.
- **Timing:** health is restored and the cost charged when time next moves.
- **Refused when:** the building is not the player's or not repairable; it is not damaged; an enemy unit is near it (within 15 tiles in a match against computer lords, 30 otherwise); or wood or stone is short.

```python
game.repair(12)
# {"queued": "repair", "building_id": 12, "wood": 0, "stone": 9, "note": "repaired to full hp when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [`building_info`](observe.md#building_info); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#repair).


## `set_building_active`

Put a type of building to sleep or wake it. [API reference](../api.md#set_building_active).

- **Arguments:** `building_id` identifies the type; `active` is `False` to sleep and `True` to wake.
- **Effect:** the game applies sleep per type: **every** owned building of that building's type sleeps or wakes together. Workers of sleeping buildings leave for the campfire as idle peasants and the buildings produce nothing. After waking, workers have to walk back before production resumes.
- **Applies to:** staffed buildings (marked in the [buildings reference](../reference/buildings.md)): woodcutter, quarry, ox tether, iron mine, pitch rig, the four farms, hunter's post, mill, bakery, brewery, inn, the five weapon workshops, chapel, church, cathedral, apothecary, well and water pot.
- **Timing:** when time next moves. Nothing is queued if the type is already in the requested state.
- **Refused when:** the ID is not one of the player's buildings, `active` is not a Boolean, or the type has no sleep control.

```python
game.set_building_active(12, False)
# {"queued": "set_building_active", "type": "woodcutter", "active": False, "note": "every woodcutter of yours sleeps from when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [`building_info`](observe.md#building_info); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#set_building_active).


## `set_workshop_product`

Choose which weapon a workshop makes. [API reference](../api.md#set_workshop_product).

- **Products:** a `fletcher` makes `bows` or `crossbows`, a `poleturner` `spears` or `pikes`, a `blacksmith` `maces` or `swords`. The armourer and tanner have a single product.
- **Effect and timing:** the workshop switches from its next piece of work; a weapon already in progress is finished first. The setting applies to that one workshop.
- **Refused when:** the building is not an owned fletcher, poleturner or blacksmith; the weapon is not one of its two products; or the map does not allow that weapon to be made.

```python
game.set_workshop_product(12, "crossbows")
# {"queued": "set_workshop_product", "building_id": 12, "weapon": "crossbows", "note": "it makes this from its next piece of work"}
```

See also: [`building_info`](observe.md#building_info); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#set_workshop_product).


## `set_food_allowed`

Allow or forbid the population to eat one food. [API reference](../api.md#set_food_allowed).

- **Arguments:** `food` is `apples`, `cheese`, `meat` or `bread`; `allowed` is a Boolean.
- **Needs:** an owned granary.
- **Effect:** a forbidden food stays in the granary and is not eaten, which lowers the number of food types eaten and so the variety bonus. It does not sell or remove the food. The change is applied on the next frame without waiting for time to move, and persists until changed back.
- **Refused when:** the food name is not one of the four, `allowed` is not a Boolean, there is no granary, or the game mode does not have the granary's food controls.

```python
game.set_food_allowed("bread", False)
# {"food": "bread", "allowed": False}
```

See also: [`report`](observe.md#report); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#set_food_allowed).

<!-- docs/commands/military.md -->

# Military commands

These commands give orders to the player's units: movement, stance, patrols and attacks. Rules shared by all of them:

- **Unit IDs.** `unit_ids` is a list of 1 to 500 distinct IDs of the player's own live units, taken from `state()["units"]` where `owner` is 1. Soldiers, the lord and crewed siege engines all qualify. Although the client's signature allows `None`, the driver requires an explicit list. An ID that is not a live own unit refuses the whole command (`unit N is not one of your live soldiers`).
- **Grouping.** Each order selects exactly the listed units as one group and gives the group the order, as a selection and click in the game would. A new order replaces the group's previous one.
- **Timing.** Orders are queued and the units act when time next moves. Walking takes time: advance, then read positions from state.
- **Refusals.** Every command here is refused after the match has ended (`game over: ...`) or once a configured tick budget is spent.
- **Autonomy.** Units also fight enemies that come near without orders, according to their stance.

IDs and coordinates in examples are illustrative.

## `move`

Order units to walk to a tile, optionally continuing through waypoints. [API reference](../api.md#move).

- **Arguments:** `(x, y)` is the destination tile. `waypoints` is an optional list of 1 to 8 further `(x, y)` tiles, walked in order after `(x, y)`; the game keeps at most 9 markers in all. The units stay at the last marker.
- **Limits:** units stop short of a tile they cannot reach (water, walls, enclosed ground) without an error; check their positions after advancing. In a historical campaign the lord can only be sent back to his keep.
- **Returns:** `queued`, `units` (count) and either `x`, `y` or, with waypoints, `markers` (the full route).
- **Refused when:** a tile is off the map or not a pair of integers, or the marker count is outside 2 to 9 when waypoints are given.

```python
game.move([12, 13], 230, 225, waypoints=[(235, 225)])
# {"queued": "move", "units": 2, "markers": [[230, 225], [235, 225]], "note": "they walk the markers in order when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [`state`](observe.md#state); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#move).


## `set_stance`

Set how units react to nearby enemies. [API reference](../api.md#set_stance).

- **Stances:** `stand_ground` keeps units on their spot; `defensive` lets them engage enemies that come close; `aggressive` sends them after enemies that come near.
- **Effect:** applies to exactly the listed units, from when time next moves, until changed.
- **Refused when:** `stance` is not one of the three names.

```python
game.set_stance([12, 13], "defensive")
# {"queued": "stance", "units": 2, "stance": "defensive"}
```

See also: [`stop`](#stop); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#set_stance).


## `stop`

Stop units where they are and cancel their current order. [API reference](../api.md#stop).

- **Effect:** the units halt when time next moves. Their stance still governs how they react to enemies.

```python
game.stop([12, 13])
# {"queued": "stop", "units": 2, "note": "they stop when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [`move`](#move); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#stop).


## `disband`

Turn soldiers back into peasants. [API reference](../api.md#disband).

- **Effect:** the units become peasants and walk to the campfire, where they can take jobs or be recruited again. The gold, weapons and armor they cost are not refunded.
- **Refused when:** the list includes the lord (`your lord cannot be disbanded`).

```python
game.disband([12, 13])
# {"queued": "disband", "units": 2, "note": "they turn back into peasants when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [`recruit`](economy.md#recruit); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#disband).


## `patrol`

Order units to walk a route back and forth. [API reference](../api.md#patrol).

- **Arguments:** `points` is a list of 1 to 9 `(x, y)` tiles.
- **Effect:** the units walk the points in order and back, repeatedly, until they receive another order.
- **Refused when:** `points` is not a list of 1 to 9 integer pairs or a point is off the map. In a historical campaign the lord cannot patrol.

```python
game.patrol([12, 13], [(230, 225), (235, 225)])
# {"queued": "patrol", "units": 2, "points": [[230, 225], [235, 225]]}
```

See also: [`move`](#move); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#patrol).


## `attack_ground`

Order ranged units to keep shooting at a tile. [API reference](../api.md#attack_ground).

- **Units:** ranged soldiers only: archers, crossbowmen, slingers, horse archers, Arabian archers and fire throwers.
- **Effect:** the units shoot at the spot from where they stand, hitting whatever enters it, and pay less attention to enemies elsewhere than idle ranged units do. The order lasts until replaced.
- **Refused when:** a listed unit is not ranged, or the tile is off the map.

```python
game.attack_ground([12, 13], 240, 230)
# {"queued": "attack_ground", "units": 2, "x": 240, "y": 230}
```

See also: [`attack`](#attack); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#attack_ground).


## `attack_wall`

Order units to attack an enemy wall tile. [API reference](../api.md#attack_wall).

- **Arguments:** `(x, y)` must be a wall tile (`^` on the map) owned by a player who is neither the controlled player nor an ally.
- **Effect:** the units walk to the wall and attack that tile. A siege tower given this order rolls to the wall and docks, letting soldiers climb onto the wall over it.
- **Refused when:** the tile is not a wall tile, or the wall is the player's own or an ally's.

```python
game.attack_wall([12, 13], 240, 230)
# {"queued": "attack_wall", "units": 2, "x": 240, "y": 230}
```

See also: [`attack_building`](#attack_building); [`set_ladder`](siege.md#set_ladder); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#attack_wall).


## `attack`

Order units to attack one enemy unit. [API reference](../api.md#attack).

- **Arguments:** `target_id` is the ID of a live unit of another, non-allied player from `state()["units"]`. An enemy lord's ID is in `state()["enemy"]["lords"]`.
- **Effect:** the units pursue and attack the target. When it dies they fall back on their stance; give a new order for the next target.
- **Refused when:** the target is not a live enemy unit of a recognized type, or belongs to an ally.

```python
game.attack([12, 13], target_id=42)
# {"queued": "attack", "units": 2, "target_id": 42, "note": "they attack when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [`state`](observe.md#state); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#attack).


## `attack_building`

Order units to attack one enemy building. [API reference](../api.md#attack_building).

- **Arguments:** `building_id` is the `id` of an entry in `state()["enemy"]["buildings"]`.
- **Effect:** the units walk to the building and attack it until it is destroyed. A keep cannot be damaged. Catapults and trebuchets shoot buildings from range; a battering ram walks up and batters.
- **Refused when:** the ID is not a building of another, non-allied player.

```python
game.attack_building([12, 13], building_id=42)
# {"queued": "attack", "units": 2, "building_id": 42, "note": "they attack when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [`state`](observe.md#state); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#attack_building).

<!-- docs/commands/observe.md -->

# Observe commands

These commands read the game: state, map, building sites, events and the game's information panels. They are not limited by a tick budget. After the game has ended the match, only `state` still answers; the others are refused with `game over: ...`. IDs and coordinates in examples are illustrative.

## `state`

Return the current visible game state. [API reference](../api.md#state).

- **Returns:** one `State` snapshot: clock, treasury and stock, popularity, population and housing, tax and rations, the player's buildings, every recognized unit on the map, and in a skirmish the enemy lords and buildings. Every field is described in the [state reference](../reference/state.md).
- **Use:** take unit and building IDs from it immediately before ordering; unit IDs are reused after a unit dies.
- **Refusals:** none from the driver; it also answers after the match has ended.

```python
s = game.state()
archers = [u["id"] for u in s["units"] if u["owner"] == 1 and u["type"] == "archer"]
print(s["tick"], s["gold"], s["stock"]["wood"], s["popularity"], s["idle_peasants"])
```

See also: [state reference](../reference/state.md); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#state).


## `map`

Return the inclusive tile rectangle as text. [API reference](../api.md#map).

- **Arguments:** `x0, y0, x1, y1`, each 0 to 399 with `x0 <= x1` and `y0 <= y1`. The default is the whole 400 × 400 map.
- **Returns:** newline-separated rows, one character per tile. Row 0 of the result is `y0` and column 0 is `x0`, so `rows[y - y0][x - x0]` is tile `(x, y)`. The characters are explained in the [map legend](../reference/map-legend.md): `.` open ground, `,` farmable grass, `~` water, `^` blocked or wall, letters for buildings.
- **Limits:** the map shows terrain and buildings, not units, and not builds queued in the current pause.
- **Refused when:** a coordinate is not an integer in range or the rectangle is inverted (`invalid map rectangle`).

```python
rows = game.map(220, 220, 240, 240).splitlines()
tile = rows[230 - 220][235 - 220]  # tile (235, 230)
```

See also: [map legend](../reference/map-legend.md); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#map).


## `find_sites`

Find positions where the game would accept a building now, nearest first. [API reference](../api.md#find_sites).

- **Arguments:** `building` is a placement name from the [buildings reference](../reference/buildings.md), `keep`, or a siege engine name (for its 3 × 3 tent). `limit` is 1 to 50 (default 5). `near` is the tile to search around; without it the search centres on tile (235, 230), so pass a tile near the player's keep or the resource wanted.
- **Returns:** up to `limit` sites as `{"x", "y"}` top-left tiles, nearest to `near` first, none overlapping another or a build queued in this pause. Every site has passed the map checks and the game's own placement check.
- **Limits:** the driver tests at most `10 * limit` candidates against the game, so the list can be shorter than `limit`, or empty, even when valid spots exist farther away; raise `limit` or move `near`. Cost is not checked, and a site can stop being free once time moves.
- **Refused when:** the name is not a recognized placement name, `limit` is out of range, or the map's build menu does not offer the building.

```python
sites = game.find_sites("wheat_farm", limit=3, near=(235, 230))
# [{"x": 228, "y": 236}, {"x": 240, "y": 221}]
if sites:
    game.build("wheat_farm", sites[0]["x"], sites[0]["y"])
```

See also: [`build`](economy.md#build); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#find_sites).


## `look`

Centre the camera on a tile. Always refused by the game driver. [API reference](../api.md#look).

- **Refusals:** every call fails with `camera control is not supported`. The whole map is readable through `state` and `map` without moving a camera, so nothing depends on this command.

```python
game.look(235, 230)  # raises CrusaderError
```

See also: [how it works](../how-it-works.md); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#look).


## `select`

Select owned units by ID, as a drag-select in the game does. [API reference](../api.md#select).

- **Arguments:** a list of 1 to 500 distinct IDs of the player's own live units.
- **Effect:** replaces the game's current selection and groups the units. Every order command selects its own units, so `select` is never required before an order.
- **Returns:** `{"tribe": n}`, the group number the game assigned.
- **Refused when:** the list is empty, too long or has duplicates, or an ID is not one of the player's live units.

```python
game.select([12, 13])
# {"tribe": 1249}
```

See also: [`move`](military.md#move); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#select).


## `events`

Return the session's events from a list offset onward. [API reference](../api.md#events).

- **Arguments:** `since` is an offset into the event list, 0 (the default, everything) through the current number of events. It is not a tick.
- **Returns:** a list of event objects, oldest first; `[]` when nothing is new. Each has `type` and `tick` plus the fields of its type; see the [events reference](../reference/events.md).
- **Use:** keep a count of events read and pass it as `since` after each `advance`.
- **Refused when:** `since` is negative, beyond the event count or not an integer (`invalid event offset`), and after the match has ended.

```python
seen = 0
game.advance(800)
for event in game.events(since=seen):
    print(event["type"], event["tick"])
    seen += 1
```

See also: [events reference](../reference/events.md); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#events).


## `report`

Return one page of the game's information book. [API reference](../api.md#report).

`page` selects the figures returned:

| Page | Fields |
|---|---|
| `popularity` | `food`, `tax`, `crowding`, `fear_factor`, `religion`, `ale_coverage`: each factor's monthly popularity change in the units the game displays; `coming_month`: their sum. Optional `event_0` to `event_5` and `event_flag` appear while a scripted map event affects popularity. |
| `fear` | `good_things`, `bad_things` (counts built), `popularity_effect` (the fear level, −5 to 5), `next_level_in` (how many more are needed for the next level; absent at ±5), `efficiency_pct` (worker efficiency). |
| `religion` | `priests`, `blessed_pct`, `popularity_effect`, `next_level_at` (blessed percentage of the next step; absent from 95 %). |
| `army` | `troops`: `{unit name: count}` of the player's live troops and engines, without the lord; `fear_bonus`: combat modifier in percent, 5 per fear level. |
| `food` | `meat`, `cheese`, `bread`, `apples`: granary stock. |
| `population` | `history`: population at the end of each game month so far (at most 300 values). |
| `stores` | `wood`, `hops`, `stone`, `iron`, `pitch`, `wheat`, `ale`, `flour`: stockpile stock. |
| `weapons` | `bows`, `crossbows`, `spears`, `pikes`, `maces`, `swords`, `leather_armor`, `metal_armor`: armory stock. |
| `merit` | `lords`: one `{player, gold, troops}` per lord still in the game, the game's Order of Merit. |

- **Refused when:** `page` is not one of the nine names.

```python
game.report("popularity")
# {"food": 4, "tax": -2, "crowding": 0, "fear_factor": 0, "religion": 0, "ale_coverage": 0, "coming_month": 2}
```

The popularity factors are explained in the [mechanics primer](../concepts.md#popularity).

See also: [state reference](../reference/state.md); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#report).


## `building_info`

Return what the game's panel shows for one of the player's buildings. [API reference](../api.md#building_info).

- **Arguments:** `building_id` from `state()["buildings"]`. Other players' buildings have no panel.
- **Returns:** always `id` and `type`, then by building type:

| Building | Extra fields |
|---|---|
| `hovel` | `houses`: 8. |
| `granary` | `food_units` (total food), `months_supply` (`None` when the game shows none), `food_types_eaten`, `rations`, `rations_popularity` and `variety_popularity` (the two food factors, in displayed popularity units). The figures describe the whole town, not one granary. |
| `keep` | `peasants` (population) and `tax` (level −3 to 8). |
| towers and gatehouses | `hp`, `max_hp`. |
| `fletcher`, `poleturner`, `blacksmith` | `status`: the panel's status lines as text, when it shows any. |
| any staffed building | `worker`: the panel's worker line in the game's own words (for example that there is no worker, that it sleeps, or what the worker is doing). Absent when the panel has none. |

- **Refused when:** the ID is not an integer or not one of the player's buildings (`building N is not one of yours`).

```python
game.building_info(31)
# {"id": 31, "type": "granary", "food_units": 62, "months_supply": 5, "food_types_eaten": 2,
#  "rations": "normal", "rations_popularity": 0, "variety_popularity": 1}
```

See also: [buildings reference](../reference/buildings.md); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#building_info).

<!-- docs/commands/siege.md -->

# Siege commands

These commands build and crew siege engines and direct the specialist troops of an assault: laddermen and tunnelers. Engines are units and, once crewed, take the [military commands](military.md) (`move`, `attack`, `attack_building`, `attack_wall`) with their own unit ID. Unit lists follow the same rules as military commands: 1 to 500 distinct IDs of the player's own live units. Every command is queued for when time next moves and is refused after the match has ended or a tick budget is spent. IDs and coordinates in examples are illustrative.

## `build_siege`

Have engineers put up a siege tent and build an engine in it. [API reference](../api.md#build_siege).

- **Arguments:** `engineer_ids` are engineers; `engine` is `catapult`, `trebuchet`, `battering_ram`, `siege_tower`, `portable_shield` or `fire_ballista`; `(x, y)` is the top-left tile of the 3 × 3 tent. `find_sites(engine)` returns tent sites.
- **Cost:** gold from the game's cost table, charged when time next moves: 150 for every engine except the portable shield (5) in game version 1.41. The result's `gold` field is the amount.
- **Crew:** catapult 2, trebuchet 3, battering ram 4, siege tower 4, portable shield 1, fire ballista 2. The engineers who build the engine become its crew. Send at least the crew size: an engine built by fewer comes out uncrewed and takes no orders until `man` completes its crew. Extra engineers stay free.
- **Timing:** the tent appears when time moves; the engineers walk to it and build, and the engine appears on the tent's tile as a unit in `State.units` a few hundred ticks later (roughly 300 to 600).
- **Refused when:** the engine name is not recognized or the map's siege menu does not offer it; a listed unit is not an engineer; the tent site fails the map check or the game's placement check (for example too close to the enemy); or gold is short.
- **Afterwards:** a `build_refused` event is recorded if the tent could not be placed when time moved.

```python
engineers = [u["id"] for u in game.state()["units"] if u["owner"] == 1 and u["type"] == "engineer"][:2]
site = game.find_sites("catapult", limit=1, near=(220, 200))[0]
game.build_siege(engineers, "catapult", site["x"], site["y"])
# {"queued": "build_siege", "engine": "catapult", "x": 220, "y": 198, "gold": 150, "note": "..."}
```

See also: [siege engines](../reference/units.md#siege-engines); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#build_siege).


## `man`

Send engineers to crew an owned engine that is short of crew. [API reference](../api.md#man).

- **Arguments:** `engineer_ids` are free engineers; `engine_id` is an own siege engine or tower engine from `state()["units"]`.
- **Effect:** as many of the engineers as the engine still needs walk to it and board. Crew is all or nothing: an engine acts only with its full crew, so send enough engineers to complete it. The result's `crew_needed` is the number still missing when the order was given.
- **Tower engines:** a `mangonel` or `ballista` needs 2 engineers, who must be able to walk up to it: the tower has to be joined to a wall with stairs to the ground.
- **Refused when:** a listed unit is not an engineer; `engine_id` is not one of the player's engines; the engine already has its full crew; or the engineers cannot reach it.

```python
game.man([101, 102], 205)
# {"queued": "man", "engine_id": 205, "crew_needed": 2, "note": "they walk to it when game time next moves"}
```

See also: [`unman`](#unman); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#man).


## `unman`

Take the crew off an owned engine. [API reference](../api.md#unman).

- **Effect:** the engineers step off and are free for other work. The engine stays where it is and takes no orders until crewed again.
- **Refused when:** `engine_id` is not one of the player's engines, or it has no crew.

```python
game.unman(205)
# {"queued": "unman", "engine_id": 205}
```

See also: [`man`](#man); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#unman).


## `buy_ammo`

Buy 20 shots for a catapult or trebuchet for 10 stone. [API reference](../api.md#buy_ammo).

- **Applies to:** own catapults and trebuchets. A catapult starts with 20 shots and uses one per shot; `State.units` shows the remaining `ammo`.
- **Cost and timing:** 10 stone from the stockpile for 20 more shots, taken when time next moves.
- **Refused when:** the unit is not an own catapult or trebuchet, or the stockpile holds fewer than 10 stone.

```python
game.buy_ammo(205)
# {"queued": "buy_ammo", "engine_id": 205, "stone": 10, "shots": 20}
```

See also: [`attack_building`](military.md#attack_building); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#buy_ammo).


## `throw_cow`

Order a catapult or trebuchet to throw a cow at a tile. [API reference](../api.md#throw_cow).

- **Needs:** a crewed own catapult or trebuchet, and at least one cow. Cows are the cattle of the player's dairy farms; own catapults and trebuchets show the count as `cows` in state.
- **Effect:** the crew throws one cow at `(x, y)`; the carcass lies where it lands, and the cow count drops by one. The result's `cows` is the count when the order was given.
- **Refused when:** the unit is not an own catapult or trebuchet, it has no crew, the player has no cows, or the tile is off the map.

```python
game.throw_cow(205, 80, 70)
# {"queued": "throw_cow", "engine_id": 205, "x": 80, "y": 70, "cows": 3}
```

See also: [`buy_ammo`](#buy_ammo); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#throw_cow).


## `set_ladder`

Order laddermen to raise a ladder against an enemy wall tile. [API reference](../api.md#set_ladder).

- **Arguments:** `unit_ids` are laddermen; `(x, y)` is a wall tile (`^` on the map) of a player who is neither the controlled player nor an ally.
- **Effect:** the laddermen carry a ladder to the wall and raise it; soldiers ordered onto or over the wall can then climb there. Laddermen cannot fight.
- **Refused when:** a listed unit is not a ladderman, the tile is not a wall tile, or the wall is the player's own or an ally's.

```python
game.set_ladder([301], 80, 70)
# {"queued": "set_ladder", "units": 1, "x": 80, "y": 70}
```

See also: [`attack_wall`](military.md#attack_wall); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#set_ladder).


## `dig_tunnel`

Order tunnelers to start a tunnel at a tile. [API reference](../api.md#dig_tunnel).

- **Arguments:** `unit_ids` are tunnelers; `(x, y)` is the top-left tile of the tunnel entrance.
- **Effect:** a tunneler digs underground from the entrance toward the nearest enemy wall or building; when the tunnel collapses under it, that wall tile is destroyed or the building damaged.
- **Placement:** the game accepts an entrance only where an enemy-built wall or a small enemy tower lies within tunnelling distance; the walls that come with an enemy keep do not count. Against an enemy who has built no walls every spot is refused.
- **Refused when:** a listed unit is not a tunneler, the tile is off the map, or the game refuses the spot (often without stating a reason).

```python
game.dig_tunnel([302], 75, 70)
# {"queued": "dig_tunnel", "units": 1, "x": 75, "y": 70}
```

See also: [`attack_wall`](military.md#attack_wall); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#dig_tunnel).

<!-- docs/commands/time.md -->

# Time commands

The game is paused between calls. `advance` is the only command that moves time, and the point at which every queued command takes effect.

## `advance`

Run the game for 1 to 3000 ticks. [API reference](../api.md#advance).

- **Arguments:** `ticks` is an integer from 1 to 3000. A month is 800 ticks; call `advance` repeatedly for longer spans.
- **Effect:** queued builds, trades, recruits and orders are applied as time starts to move, then the game runs. The driver stops exactly at the requested tick, or earlier if the game ends the match or a configured tick budget runs out.
- **Returns:** `tick` (the session tick now), `ticks_left` (the remaining budget, or `None` when no budget is configured) and `game_over` (`None`, `"match won"` or `"match lost"`). The call returns only these three fields; read what happened with `events` and `state`.
- **Events:** at each 800-tick boundary a `month_end` event is recorded and the lords are checked; after the call, builds and demolitions that the game did not carry out are recorded as `build_refused` and `demolish_refused`.
- **Duration:** a call returns when the ticks have run, which takes real time; the client's default request timeout is 600 seconds.
- **Refused when:** `ticks` is not an integer from 1 to 3000, the match has ended, or the tick budget is spent.

```python
result = game.advance(800)
# {"tick": 800, "ticks_left": None, "game_over": None}
for event in game.events():
    print(event["type"])
```

See also: [`events`](observe.md#events); [time and pause](../concepts.md#time-and-pause); [refusals](../reference/errors.md#advance).

<!-- docs/concepts.md -->

# Concepts

## Time and pause

The game is paused between calls and moves only inside `advance(ticks)`, which runs 1 to 3000 ticks and returns the current tick, the remaining budget if one is configured, and the game-over status. A match can end before the requested interval. A month is exactly 800 ticks. Most commands are queued: the game applies them when time next moves, so advance and read state again before relying on an effect. Several commands can be queued in one pause; the driver tracks the gold, goods, peasants and tiles they will use, so a later command in the same pause is refused if an earlier one has already claimed what it needs.

## Coordinates and IDs

Map coordinates are tile `(x, y)` pairs on a 400 × 400 grid; map rectangles are inclusive. A building's coordinates identify the top-left tile of its square footprint. Use `find_sites` to find positions the game accepts, then handle refusal because conditions can change. Unit and building IDs come from state; they belong to the current match, and unit IDs are reused after a unit dies. Orders need owned units or buildings. Player 1 is the controlled player; other numbers are computer lords.

## Events and refusals

`events(since)` takes an offset into the session's event list; after reading a batch, advance the offset by its length. Event fields vary by type. `advance` does not return events; read them with `events`. See [events](reference/events.md).

A command is refused when its arguments are invalid or the game would not allow the action; the client raises `CrusaderError` with the reason, which is usually specific enough to act on (for example the amounts a build needs and the amounts held). A successful request means the command was queued, not that it achieved its aim: a unit can walk onto a building site, or a path can be blocked. Inspect subsequent state and events. After the game ends a match, every command except `state` is refused. See [errors](reference/errors.md).

## Game mechanics primer

This section summarizes the rules of Stronghold Crusader that matter when playing through the SDK. Figures come from the game's own panels as the driver reads them, unless marked as measured or taken from the game manual.

### Peasants, housing and jobs

The town's population is its peasants. New peasants walk in from the map edge while popularity is 50 or more and housing has room; below 50 they start to leave. Each hovel houses 8. An arriving peasant waits at the campfire by the keep (`State.idle_peasants`) until a staffed building needs a worker or `recruit` turns him into a soldier. A staffed building without a worker produces nothing, so buildings, housing and popularity have to grow together. `disband` and putting buildings to sleep return people to the campfire.

### Popularity

Popularity runs from 0 to 100 and moves each month by the sum of several factors. `report("popularity")` returns each factor and their sum (`coming_month`) in the units the game displays:

| Factor | Values |
|---|---|
| Food (rations) | `none` −8, `half` −4, `normal` 0, `extra` +4, `double` +8. An empty granary counts as −8 whatever the setting. |
| Food (variety) | Eating 2 food types +1, 3 types +2, all 4 types +3. |
| Tax | Level −3: +7, −2: +5, −1: +3, 0: +1, 1: −2, 2: −4, 3: −6, 4: −8, 5: −12, 6: −16, 7: −20, 8: −24. A bribe level with an empty treasury counts as +1. |
| Crowding | 0 while the game's crowding figure is at or below 100 %; −2 for each further 20 %, down to −10. Build hovels before the town outgrows them. |
| Fear factor | −5 to +5: the town's fear level, raised by good things and lowered by bad things. |
| Religion | By share of the population blessed: under 25 % 0, 25 % +2, 50 % +4, 75 % +6, 95 % +8; plus two further bonuses of +1 and +2, which the game manual attributes to a church and a cathedral. |
| Ale coverage | By share of the population served by inns: under 25 % 0, 25 % +2, 50 % +4, 75 % +6, 100 % +8. |

Food, tax and crowding count as 0 until the town has peasants. Scripted map events can add further lines. Popularity acts as a reserve: it can be built up with low taxes and good food and then spent on a period of high taxes, as long as it stays at 50 or above.

### Food and rations

Peasants eat apples, cheese, meat and bread from the granary; consumption grows with the population and with the ration level. Wheat and flour are not food until baked. Food only counts once a worker has delivered it to a granary, and a new granary must touch an existing one. When the granary is full, deliveries stop. `building_info(granary_id)` reports the food stock and `months_supply`. A small town eats little (measured: about 5 units a month for 34 peasants at normal rations), so an early surplus can pay for `extra` rations or be sold.

### Taxes and gold

`set_tax(level)` takes −3 to 8. Positive levels collect gold from every peasant; the game accumulates it weekly and pays it into the treasury at the end of each game month, so the first receipts arrive a month after the change. Negative levels are bribes paid out of the treasury the same way. Measured examples: level 4 yields about 48 gold a month from 40 peasants; level −3 costs about 1 gold per peasant per month. The other sources of gold are selling goods at a market and, at the start of a match, the starting treasury.

### The first month of a new skirmish

A new skirmish does not hand over its starting goods at once: the starting gold and wood are paid out gradually over roughly the first 640 ticks. Builds ordered at tick 0 can therefore be refused for lack of wood or gold. Advance most of the first month, then read `State.stock` and start building.

### Production chains

Raw-material buildings (woodcutter, quarry with ox tether, iron mine, pitch rig, farms) deliver to the stockpile or granary; processing buildings (mill, bakery, brewery, weapon workshops) fetch an input from a store and deliver the product to another. The full chains are tabulated in the [buildings reference](reference/buildings.md#production-chains). Points that decide whether a chain works:

- Every link needs its own worker and therefore a free peasant.
- Workers walk. Place producers near what they harvest and near the store they deliver to, and leave paths open: buildings packed around the keep, granary or stockpile can wall them in and stop all deliveries.
- Stores fill up. A stockpile holds a limited number of goods; extra stockpiles, granaries and armories must touch the existing one.
- Farms need farmable grass (`,` on the map), iron mines ore, quarries stone and pitch rigs marsh. `find_sites` returns only spots the game accepts.
- Output arrives in loads with long gaps (measured: a woodcutter brings about 12 wood a load; a quarry's first ox load of about 12 stone arrives several months after it is built). A month with nothing from a new building is normal.

### Fear factor

Good things (maypole, dancing bear, gardens, statue, shrine) and bad things (gallows, stocks, dungeon and the rest) move the town's fear level between −5 and +5 once there are enough of them for the town's size. Good things raise popularity each month, slow workers and strengthen troops; bad things lower popularity, speed workers up (measured at level −4: about a third more wood per woodcutter) and weaken troops. `report("fear")` shows the counts, the level, and `efficiency_pct`; `report("army")` shows the matching combat modifier as `fear_bonus`, 5 % per level.

### Soldiers and winning

Barracks troops need a weapon (and for some, armor) from the armory, gold and an idle peasant; mercenaries, engineers, laddermen, tunnelers and monks need only gold and a peasant at their building. Weapons are made by workshops or bought at the market. See [units](reference/units.md). In a skirmish each player has a lord; the game ends the match shortly after a lord dies, and `State.game_over` then reads `"match won"` or `"match lost"`. A keep cannot be damaged, so an enemy is beaten by reaching and killing his lord. Soldiers fight enemies that come near on their own according to their stance; orders direct them at a unit, building, wall tile or place.

### Castle

Stone walls cost half a stone a tile and block ground units; stairs let soldiers onto them, gatehouses let them through, and towers give ranged troops height. A moat is planned for free and dug by soldiers; a dug moat blocks ground units. Pitch ditches lit from a brazier, killing pits, dog cages and tower engines add to the defence. Attackers answer with siege engines, ladders, siege towers, tunnels and by filling moats. See the [defences](commands/defences.md) and [siege](commands/siege.md) commands.

<!-- docs/how-it-works.md -->

# How it works

The Python client sends command requests to the bridge. The bridge validates the command and arguments, serializes backend calls, and returns JSON. The real backend starts or attaches to the supported game under Linux/Wine, reads game state from process memory, and uses the included UCP3 module for tick control and a command mailbox. The module submits game commands through the game's own command queue. Some driver operations also write limited process memory directly.

## Memory boundary

The process-memory layer verifies the executable SHA-256 and that the verified file is mapped by the process, then requires a layout sanity check. It checks mappings and permissions on access, bounds each operation to a single mapped region and at most 1 MiB, and limits writes to fixed ranges or validated dynamic module regions. Dynamic hook addresses come from the module log. These checks reduce accidental misuse; they are not a security sandbox for a compromised local process or trusted driver. Arbitrary memory access is not exposed as a bridge command. The module mailbox includes in-game write and function-call primitives used by the trusted driver; a compromised same-user process or a driver bug could abuse them.

The backend depends on a specific executable and memory layout, process permissions, Wine and the module. Other versions can fail or behave incorrectly. The Docker integration is verified against the live game with `tools/smoke.py` (start from a fresh skirmish). Game state and command support are not complete; in particular, `look` is refused by the current real backend.

The container starts UCP3 with `--ucp-no-security` so it can load the unsigned local module; this also enables the UCP3 console.

<!-- docs/protocol.md -->

# Bridge protocol

The bridge serves REST and stateless streamable HTTP MCP from the same application. MCP tools use the command names and wire parameters in the [API reference](api.md); the MCP endpoint is `/mcp`. Both transports invoke the same serialized backend. `GET /health` returns `{"ok": true}` and checks the bridge, not game readiness.

## REST

Send `POST /api/{command}` with a JSON object of arguments. For example:

```sh
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/state \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

A successful response is `{"result": ...}`. An unknown command returns 404; malformed input, invalid arguments, and backend errors normally return 400 with `{"error": "..."}`. The Python `map` method uses the wire command `ascii_map`; `find_sites` sends `near_x` and `near_y` together.

Slow REST requests stream whitespace as keepalives before the final JSON object. A client must allow leading JSON whitespace and read the entire response. Once streaming has started the HTTP status is already 200, even if the final object contains an error; inspect the body. The Python client does this. Requests can take a long time: its default timeout is 600 seconds.

## Access control

The server defaults to loopback and no authentication. Configure `CRUSADER_TOKEN` to require `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on every route except `/health`, including MCP. The server also accepts `--token`, but prefer the environment variable to avoid exposing the token in command-line arguments. The Python client reads `CRUSADER_TOKEN` or accepts an explicit `token` in `Game` and `Game.connect`; the explicit value takes precedence. A token is not transport encryption; use an appropriate secure channel and do not expose an unauthenticated bridge to untrusted networks. Requests are limited to 64 KiB. All routes require a loopback `Host` by default; repeat `--allow-host` for additional host authorities. An `Origin`, if sent, must be loopback, and every POST requires `Content-Type: application/json`.

<!-- docs/quickstart.md -->

# Quickstart

## Install the client

The client requires Python 3.10 or later. From a checkout:

```sh
python -m pip install crusader-sdk   # or, from a checkout: python -m pip install .
```

The client needs a running bridge and does not start the game itself. Against a bridge on the default local address:

```python
from crusader import Game, CrusaderError

game = Game.connect()  # or Game.connect("http://127.0.0.1:8000")
try:
    print(game.state())
    print(game.map(0, 0, 20, 20))
    print(game.advance(100))
except CrusaderError as exc:
    print(f"Bridge refused the request: {exc}")
```

`CRUSADER_URL` overrides the default URL when no URL is passed. Set `CRUSADER_TOKEN` to the bridge token for authenticated requests, or pass `token=` to `Game` or `Game.connect`. Prefer the environment variable over command-line arguments for secrets. `advance` changes the game; choose a tick count appropriate for your match. See [concepts](concepts.md), the [API reference](api.md), and [protocol](protocol.md).

## Run the bridge

For a bridge installation, install the optional dependencies with `python -m pip install 'crusader-sdk[bridge]'` (or `'.[bridge]'` from a checkout), then run `crusader-bridge --help` for match and process options. The real backend requires the supported game, Wine/Linux process access, and the included UCP3 module. The `--backend module:callable` option is a development hook for selecting an explicit backend factory. Alternatively, the following experimental Docker setup packages the runtime.

## Run with Docker

This container setup is verified against the live game (`tools/smoke.py`, 12 of 12 steps on a fresh skirmish). You need Docker and your own legally obtained, supported Stronghold Crusader game folder. The image targets `linux/amd64`; other hosts require Docker's amd64 emulation.

From the repository root, verify the executable and build the image:

```sh
./scripts/check-game-files.sh "/path/to/your/game"
./scripts/build-image.sh
```

The game folder must contain `Stronghold Crusader.exe` with the supported SHA-256. The build downloads and verifies UCP3; it does not include the game. Optionally, check a UCP3 archive separately with `./scripts/check-game-files.sh "/path/to/your/game" "/path/to/UCP3.zip"`.

Set `CRUSADER_TOKEN` in the host environment, replace the example path with the absolute path to your game folder, and run:

```sh
docker run --rm --name crusader-sdk \
  --platform linux/amd64 \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  -e CRUSADER_TOKEN \
  --mount type=bind,src="/path/to/your/game",dst=/game,readonly \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 \
  crusader-sdk:local --host 0.0.0.0
```

The container needs no added capabilities: the bridge reads the game process it starts as the same user, and the live check passes with `--cap-drop ALL` alone. Do not use `--privileged` or host networking. The bridge binds to all container interfaces so Docker can publish it, but the published port is restricted to host loopback. The bridge is unauthenticated unless a token is configured; do not expose it to untrusted networks. Other containers on the same Docker network may still reach it.

Check the bridge from the host:

```sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health
```

The container copies the mounted game to `/opt/crusader` and runs the copy. The original mount remains read-only. Saves are in `/home/crusader/Stronghold Crusader/Saves` inside the container and are lost when the `--rm` container is removed. To load an existing save, place it in the source game's `Saves` folder before starting and pass `--match load:NAME` after the image name (alongside `--host 0.0.0.0`). Stop the container with `docker stop crusader-sdk`.

<!-- docs/reference/buildings.md -->

# Buildings

`build(building, x, y)` takes a placement name from the tables below; `(x, y)` is the top-left tile of a square footprint. An owned building in `State.buildings` has `id`, `type`, `x` and `y`; enemy records additionally have `owner`, `hp` and `max_hp`. A few placement names read back under another `type`, noted in the table.

## How placement is checked

`build` and `find_sites` apply the same checks, in this order. A failed check refuses the command with the reason in the error message.

1. **Map.** Every footprint tile must be on the map, be land, hold no building, unit, wall, tree, rock or farmland, not belong to a build queued earlier in the same pause, and be level with the other footprint tiles. Farms additionally need farmable grass on every tile and an iron mine needs iron ore on every tile.
2. **The game's own placement check**, the one its user interface runs. Its reasons include: a new granary, stockpile or armory must be adjacent to an existing one; too close to enemy units or buildings; too far from the castle; too close to a signpost; inaccessible land; farms need an oasis or fertile land. A spot the game refuses without a message is reported as such.
3. **Build menu.** A building the map's build menu does not offer is refused (`this mission's build menu does not offer it`).
4. **Cost.** The driver reads the cost from the game's cost table when `build` is called and refuses if the stock is short; the error states the amounts needed and held. `find_sites` does not check cost.

The costs below are the values of the supported game version (1.41); the game's table is authoritative and is what the driver charges against. The game takes the cost and places the building when time next moves. If the spot is no longer free then (usually a unit walked onto it), a `build_refused` event follows. `demolish` refunds half the cost.

## Building table

"Staffed" buildings need a peasant as worker, do nothing without one, and can be put to sleep with `set_building_active`; `building_info(id)["worker"]` reports the worker's status. "Map" is the character `map()` draws for the building. Towers and gatehouses are the only buildings with a health bar and `repair`.

| Building | Footprint | Cost | Placement | Staffed | Map | Purpose |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| `woodcutter` | 3 × 3 | 3 wood | free flat land | yes | `w` | Its worker fells nearby trees and carries wood to the stockpile. Place it near trees (`^`). |
| `stockpile` | 5 × 5 | free | free flat land; the game requires an additional stockpile to touch an existing one | no | `s` | Stores wood, hops, stone, iron, pitch, wheat, flour and ale. More stockpiles give more room; goods with no room are not delivered. |
| `hovel` | 4 × 4 | 6 wood | free flat land | no | `h` | Housing for 8 peasants (`State.housing` rises by 8). |
| `quarry` | 6 × 6 | 20 wood | stone deposit (game check; use `find_sites`) | yes | `q` | Its workers cut stone, which stays at the quarry until an `ox_tether` ox carries it to the stockpile. A quarry without a tether delivers no stone. |
| `keep` | 7 × 7 | cannot be built | placed by the map | no | `K` | The lord's home and the campfire where idle peasants wait. It cannot be built, demolished or damaged; `find_sites("keep")` only reports where a 7 × 7 footprint fits. |
| `wheat_farm` | 9 × 9 | 15 wood | farmable grass (`,`) on every tile | yes | `f` | Grows wheat and delivers it to the stockpile; a mill turns it into flour. |
| `hops_farm` | 9 × 9 | 15 wood | farmable grass (`,`) on every tile | yes | `j` | Grows hops and delivers them to the stockpile; a brewery turns them into ale. |
| `apple_orchard` | 11 × 11 | 5 wood | farmable grass (`,`) on every tile | yes | `a` | Grows apples and delivers them to the granary (food). |
| `dairy_farm` | 10 × 10 | 10 wood | farmable grass (`,`) on every tile | yes | `d` | Raises cows and delivers cheese to the granary (food). Its cows also supply the tanner and are the ammunition of `throw_cow`. |
| `mill` | 3 × 3 | 20 wood | free flat land | yes | `n` | Grinds wheat from the stockpile into flour, returned to the stockpile. |
| `bakery` | 4 × 4 | 10 wood | free flat land | yes | `k` | Bakes flour from the stockpile into bread, delivered to the granary (food). |
| `brewery` | 4 × 4 | 10 wood | free flat land | yes | `b` | Brews hops from the stockpile into ale, returned to the stockpile. |
| `market` | 5 × 5 | 5 wood | free flat land | no | `m` | Required by `trade`. It makes nothing itself. |
| `hunters_post` | 3 × 3 | 5 wood | free flat land | yes | `p` | Its hunter delivers meat to the granary (food). The game's build menu hides it in a skirmish against computer lords, where `build` refuses it. |
| `granary` | 4 × 4 | 5 wood | free flat land; the game requires a new granary to touch an existing one | no | `g` | Stores apples, cheese, meat and bread. Food counts, and is eaten, only from a granary; rations and the food toggles are its panel. |
| `armory` | 4 × 4 | 5 wood | free flat land; the game requires an additional armory to touch an existing one | no | `B` | Stores weapons and armor. Barracks recruits take their equipment from it. |
| `barracks` | 4 × 4 | 15 stone | free flat land | no | `B` | Required to recruit archers, crossbowmen, spearmen, pikemen, macemen, swordsmen and knights. |
| `inn` | 5 × 5 | 20 wood, 100 gold | free flat land | yes | `i` | Its innkeeper fetches ale from the stockpile and serves it; ale coverage of 25 % or more of the population raises popularity. |
| `chapel` | 6 × 6 | 250 gold | free flat land | yes | `c` | Its priest blesses people; the blessed share of the population raises popularity (religion). |
| `church` | 9 × 9 | 500 gold | free flat land | yes | `c` | As a chapel, and the game adds a further religion bonus while one stands. |
| `well` | 3 × 3 | 30 gold | free flat land | yes | `o` | Fire fighting: its worker draws water to put out burning buildings. |
| `fletcher` | 4 × 4 | 20 wood, 100 gold | free flat land | yes | `B` | Makes bows or crossbows from wood and delivers them to the armory; choose with `set_workshop_product`. |
| `poleturner` | 4 × 4 | 10 wood, 100 gold | free flat land | yes | `B` | Makes spears or pikes from wood and delivers them to the armory; choose with `set_workshop_product`. |
| `blacksmith` | 4 × 4 | 20 wood, 200 gold | free flat land | yes | `B` | Makes maces or swords from iron and delivers them to the armory; choose with `set_workshop_product`. |
| `armourer` | 4 × 4 | 20 wood, 100 gold | free flat land | yes | `B` | Makes metal armor from iron and delivers it to the armory. |
| `tanner` | 4 × 4 | 10 wood, 100 gold | free flat land | yes | `B` | Makes leather armor from dairy-farm cows and delivers it to the armory. |
| `mercenary_post` | 4 × 4 | 10 wood | free flat land | no | `B` | Required to hire Arabian mercenaries, who cost gold and an idle peasant but no weapons. |
| `iron_mine` | 4 × 4 | 20 wood | iron ore on every tile | yes | `B` | Mines iron and delivers it to the stockpile. |
| `lookout_tower` | 3 × 3 | 10 stone | free flat land | no | `B` | Tall, narrow tower for a few ranged troops. Repairable. |
| `perimeter_tower` | 4 × 4 | 10 stone | free flat land | no | `B` | Small wall tower. Repairable. |
| `defense_turret` | 5 × 5 | 15 stone | free flat land | no | `B` | Medium wall tower. Repairable. |
| `square_tower` | 6 × 6 | 35 stone | free flat land | no | `B` | Large tower; its top can carry a `mangonel` or `ballista`. Repairable. |
| `round_tower` | 6 × 6 | 40 stone | free flat land | no | `B` | Large tower; its top can carry a `mangonel` or `ballista`. Repairable. |
| `gatehouse` | 5 × 5 | 10 stone | free flat land | no | `B` | Gate through a wall line, opened and closed with `set_gate`. Repairable. |
| `large_gatehouse` | 7 × 7 | 20 stone | free flat land | no | `B` | Larger gate, opened and closed with `set_gate`. Repairable. |
| `engineers_guild` | 5 × 5 | 10 wood, 100 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Required to recruit engineers and laddermen. |
| `tunnelers_guild` | 5 × 5 | 10 wood, 100 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Required to recruit tunnelers. |
| `stables` | 6 × 6 | 20 wood, 400 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Breeds horses for knights: about one every 400 ticks, at most four waiting per stables. |
| `cathedral` | 13 × 13 | 1000 gold | free flat land | yes | `B` | As a church with a larger religion bonus; also required to recruit monks. |
| `apothecary` | 6 × 6 | 20 wood, 150 gold | free flat land | yes | `B` | Its healer treats disease in the town (game manual). |
| `ox_tether` | 2 × 2 | 5 wood | free flat land | yes | `B` | Its ox carries stone from a quarry to the stockpile, about 12 stone a load. Place it near the quarry. |
| `pitch_rig` | 4 × 4 | wood, charged from the game's cost table (20 wood in the game manual) | marsh (game check; refused elsewhere) | yes | `B` | Draws pitch and delivers it to the stockpile. |
| `maypole` | 3 × 3 | 25 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Good thing: counts toward the fear factor's good side. |
| `dancing_bear` | 5 × 5 | 20 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Good thing. |
| `small_garden` | 2 × 2 | 30 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Good thing. Reads back as `garden`. |
| `medium_garden` | 3 × 3 | 30 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Good thing. Reads back as `garden`. |
| `large_garden` | 4 × 4 | 30 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Good thing. Reads back as `garden`. |
| `statue` | 2 × 2 | 30 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Good thing. |
| `shrine` | 2 × 2 | 30 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Good thing. |
| `gallows` | 2 × 2 | 50 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Bad thing: counts toward the fear factor's bad side. |
| `cess_pit` | 5 × 5 | 40 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Bad thing. |
| `stocks` | 3 × 3 | 45 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Bad thing. |
| `burning_stake` | 3 × 3 | 45 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Bad thing. |
| `dungeon` | 5 × 5 | 40 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Bad thing. |
| `stretching_rack` | 3 × 3 | 45 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Bad thing. |
| `gibbet` | 2 × 2 | 50 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Bad thing. |
| `chopping_block` | 3 × 3 | 45 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Bad thing. |
| `dunking_stool` | 5 × 5 | 40 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Bad thing. |
| `gatehouse_turned` | 5 × 5 | 10 stone | free flat land | no | `B` | A gatehouse with its gate on the other axis. Reads back as `gatehouse`. |
| `large_gatehouse_turned` | 7 × 7 | 20 stone | free flat land | no | `B` | A large gatehouse with its gate on the other axis. Reads back as `large_gatehouse`. |
| `drawbridge` | 5 × 5 | 10 wood | in front of the gate of an owned gatehouse, on its gate axis | no | `B` | Bridges a moat in front of a gate; raised and lowered with `set_gate`. |
| `killing_pit` | 1 × 1 | 6 wood | free flat land | no | `B` | Hidden trap that wounds enemies who walk over it. |
| `pitch_ditch` | 1 × 1 | 1 pitch | free flat land | no | `B` | One tile of pitch that burns when lit with `light_pitch`, spreading to adjoining pitch and burning units in it. |
| `dog_cage` | 3 × 3 | 10 wood, 100 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Holds war dogs, which it releases by itself when an enemy comes near. No command controls it. |
| `oil_smelter` | 4 × 4 | 10 iron, 100 gold | free flat land | no | `B` | Boils pitch from the stockpile into oil for engineers assigned with `oil_duty`. |
| `water_pot` | 4 × 4 | 60 gold | free flat land | yes | `B` | Fire-fighting station whose workers put out fires. |

## Other placement names

These names are accepted by `build` but are not buildings: they do not appear in `State.buildings`, have no footprint, and skip the map and cost-table checks above.

| Name | Where `(x, y)` must be | Cost | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `flag_1`, `flag_2`, `flag_3`, `flag_4` | top of an owned wall or tower, with no decoration there yet | free | Decoration only; it does not change the fear factor. |
| `heads` | top of an owned wall or tower, with no decoration there yet | free | Heads on spikes; decoration only. |
| `brazier` | top of an owned wall or tower, with no decoration there yet | none charged through the driver's checks | Fire source: archers within 3 tiles of a lit brazier can `light_pitch`. |
| `mangonel` | a tower-top tile of an owned `square_tower` or `round_tower` that carries no engine and has no unit on the tile | 50 gold | Tower engine that lobs stones; appears as a unit and needs 2 engineers (`man`). |
| `ballista` | as `mangonel` | 50 gold | Tower engine that shoots bolts; appears as a unit and needs 2 engineers (`man`). |

`find_sites` also accepts the six siege engine names (`catapult`, `trebuchet`, `battering_ram`, `siege_tower`, `portable_shield`, `fire_ballista`) and returns sites for the 3 × 3 siege tent that `build_siege` places. Walls, stairs and moats are not buildings; see `build_wall` and `plan_moat` in the [defences commands](../commands/defences.md).

## Production chains

| Result | Chain |
|---|---|
| Wood | `woodcutter` → stockpile |
| Stone | `quarry` → `ox_tether` → stockpile |
| Iron | `iron_mine` (on ore) → stockpile |
| Pitch | `pitch_rig` (on marsh) → stockpile |
| Apples, cheese, meat | `apple_orchard`, `dairy_farm`, `hunters_post` → granary |
| Bread | `wheat_farm` → stockpile → `mill` → stockpile → `bakery` → granary |
| Ale | `hops_farm` → stockpile → `brewery` → stockpile → `inn` |
| Bows, crossbows, spears, pikes | wood → `fletcher` or `poleturner` → armory |
| Maces, swords, metal armor | iron → `blacksmith` or `armourer` → armory |
| Leather armor | `dairy_farm` cows → `tanner` → armory |

Each step is carried on foot by the building's worker, so distance to the stockpile, granary or armory sets the output rate, and a full store stops deliveries. See the [goods reference](goods.md) and the mechanics primer in [concepts](../concepts.md#game-mechanics-primer).
